messages.author: cd58511bd9115a1c
messages.subject: Vectorizing with point-wise exponentiation
parts:
Hi there!

 I'm trying to speed up my code by using vectorization, however it would involve point-wise exponentiation of the vector. From this old thread, it seems like that is not possible and thus vectorization of this problem would not increase efficiency. I was wondering if anyone had any ideas.

My current situation is something like this (forgive the pseudocode):

data {
int N1;
int N2;

vector xvals[N2];

matrix[N1,N2] mymat
}

parameters{
real a;
real b;
...
real sigma;
}

model{
...
for (n1 in 1:N1)
   for (n2 in 1:N2)
        mymat[n1,n2] ~ normal(a*xvals[n2]^2 + b*xvals[n2]^3 + ....., sigma);
...
}

and I'd like to speed it up by doing some sort of vectorization like this:

data {
int N1;
int N2;

vector xvals[N2];

vector[N1] mymat[N2]

}

parameters{
real a;
real b;
...
real sigma;
}


model{
...
for (n1 in 1:N1)
        x[n1] ~ normal(a*xvals^2 + b*xvals^3 + ....., sigma); //This is not a valid line of code
...
}

I don't see a way around having to loop through all the elements. In a language like matlab, I could do:

x(n1,:)= myfun(a*xvals.^2 + b*xvals.^3 ....);

But this does not seem possible in Stan.

Any thoughts?

Thanks!

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Vectorizing with point-wise exponentiation
parts:
On Wednesday, September 14, 2016 at 5:20:21 PM UTC-4, ralphe...@gmail.com wrote:
I don't see a way around having to loop through all the elements. In a language like matlab, I could do:

x(n1,:)= myfun(a*xvals.^2 + b*xvals.^3 ....);

But this does not seem possible in Stan.

Any thoughts?

Well, you could do the exponentiation once in the transformed data block and that would help a lot. However, raw polynomials tend not to work well in Stan because a and b are highly dependent with different scales. Orthogonal polynomials work much better.

You will have to loop over mymat anyway, in which case it is faster to access mymat if it is an array of vectors (as in your second example) rather than a matrix (as in your first example).

Ben

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Vectorizing with point-wise exponentiation
parts:
When you call the vectorized version of a univariate probability distribution with an argument that's meant to be broadcast, there's actually a lot of computational savings.

I'll try to explain that first sentence a bit. I'm assuming you have N1 x N2 observations (either matrix or array of vectors; the count is what matters), scalar a (single value), scalar b (single value), and scalar sigma (single value). I'm basing this off your original post. I'm assuming you want to do something like (from OP, psuedocode):

for (n1 in 1:N1)
   for (n2 in 1:N2)
        mymat[n1,n2] ~ normal(a*xvals[n2]^2 + b*xvals[n2]^3 + ....., sigma);
Let's try to get down to the computation of what happens here. This is really:

for (n1 in 1:N1)
   for (n2 in 1:N2)

target += normal_lpdf(mymat[n1,n2] | a*xvals[n2]^2 + b*xvals[n2]^3 + ....., sigma);

Nothing tricky so far. I'm going to set some local variables to help:
for (n1 in 1:N1)

for (n2 in 1:N2) {
        real y;
        real mu;
        y = mymat[n1, n2];
        mu = a*xvals[n2]^2 + b*xvals[n2]^3 + .....;
        target += normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma);
   }

Now, let's pretend we wanted to write this out by hand.
for (n1 in 1:N1)

for (n2 in 1:N2) {
        real y;
        real mu;
        y = mymat[n1, n2];
        mu = a*xvals[n2]^2 + b*xvals[n2]^3 + .....;
        target += - (y - mu)^2 / (sigma * sigma) - log(sigma) / 2 - log(2 * pi()) / 2;
   }

Do you see the repeated computation within the double for loop? That's really wasteful. I'm going to bold some of the repeated calls.
for (n1 in 1:N1)

for (n2 in 1:N2) {
        real y;
        real mu;
        y = mymat[n1, n2];
        mu = a*xvals[n2]^2 + b*xvals[n2]^3 + .....;
        target += - (y - mu)^2 / (sigma * sigma) - log(sigma) / 2 - log(2 * pi()) / 2;
   }


When our distributions are vectorized and we assume broadcasting (that's when sigma is a scalar, but since mu and sigma have N1 x N2 length, it's as if we repeat sigma N1 x N2 times), this is conceptually what happens:
real inv_sigma_sq;
real log_sigma_div_2;
inv_sigma_sq = 1 / (sigma * sigma);
log_sigma_div_2 = log(sigma) / 2;
for (n1 in 1:N1)

for (n2 in 1:N2) {
        real y;
        real mu;
        y = mymat[n1, n2];
        mu = a*xvals[n2]^2 + b*xvals[n2]^3 + .....;
        target += - (y - mu)^2 * inv_sigma_sq - log_sigma_div_2;
   }

(I dropped the constant because it's not needed.) 
Notice the expensive repeated calls get moved outside the loop? The computational efficiency of vectorized distributions happen when you have broadcasted arguments. When the sizes of the arguments are all the same, there's no computational advantage.


I hope that clarifies some of the reasons for using vectorization. Here's what I would do with your model:

matrix[N1, N2] mu;

for (n1 in 1:N1)
  for (n2 in 1:N2)

mu[n1, n2] = a*xvals[n2]^2 + b*xvals[n2]^3 + .....;
to_vector(mymat) ~ normal(to_vector(mu), sigma);

By creating a temporary matrix for the mean of the normal distribution of the same size as mymat, you can now flatten both data structures to vectors and use the vectorized call.



Daniel

> On Sep 15, 2016, at 12:24 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> target += normal_lpdf(a | a_hat, sigma_a);
> target += normal_lpdf(b | b_hat, sigma_b);
> target += normal_lpdf(x | x_hat, sigma);
>

Also, the sampling form

a ~ normal(a | a_hat, sigma_a);

can drop constants, so it's a bit more efficient, especially if
any of sigma_a, sigma_b or sigma are fixed. Probably not noticeably
faster if they're all parameters or transfomred parameters.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Vectorizing with point-wise exponentiation
parts:
normal_lpdf(y | mu, sigma) is the function that returns the log
PDF, whereas y ~ normal(y | mu, sigma) increments the log density
with the value of the log PDF (the latter sampling notation also
drops additive constants that don't depend on parameters).

- Bob

Here is my actual file, which I've tried to improve given Daniel's suggestions. This doesn't seem to speed things up too much. The goal of this model is to fit two time-varying peaks (each with their own independent parameters) to a surface.

I'm wondering if there's still any way to further optimize this code. Given that the base of the exponents are dynamic and dependent on the previous time step, I don't think they can be easily pre-computed. Also, since the ^ operator is not vectorized I can't see how to easily vectorize this problem.

Any thoughts? I truly appreciate all of your help!

-M
